items.title: The Signature That Never Comes: Why Somalia's Clan Killers Walk Free
items.description: A death sentence in Somalia isn't final until the president signs it. Increasingly, none of them do.   That piece traced how Ahmed Shire Hussein, a Somali National Army soldier, was executed on camera near El Baraf for the crime of his father's clan — one entry in a pattern of hit squads, informant networks, and a tribal shield strong enough that a court willing to execute Al-Shabaab fighters would not touch a killer protected by his own sub-clan. Why does almost no one ever pay for it? This is the answer: what decides whether the state acts is the relative political power of the clans in
items.titleIt: The Signature That Never Comes: Why Somalia's Clan Killers Walk Free

items.title: Somalia: Blood, Blades, and Broken Streets: Inside the Terror Colonizing Mogadishu
items.description: Speaking after his son's funeral at Muuse Boqor Mosque the following day, veteran journalist Maxamed Cumar Baakaay put words to what the killing meant: "Allah gave me my son, and now Allah has taken him back. I praise Him. We have survived so many historic atrocities here in Mogadishu, only for me to lose my boy to the blades of the Ciyaal Weero." Family members say police have since detained several suspects, though authorities have not issued an official statement confirming the arrests. A journalist mourning his university-bound son has shattered the illusion of security in central Mogadish
items.titleIt: Somalia: Blood, Blades, and Broken Streets: Inside the Terror Colonizing Mogadishu

items.title: The Anatomy of a Blood Debt: How Clan Revenge Killings are Fracturing Somalia's Frontlines
items.description: Before he was executed, a chilling video captured his final moments. Stranded and defenseless, Hussein looked directly at his armed captors and uttered a devastating plea: "Abtiyaalow, ha i dilina" ("Maternal uncles, do not kill me"). The phrase was not just a desperate cry for mercy — according to clan elders and opposition figures interviewed for this piece, it reflected a specific and devastating reality. items.titleIt: The Anatomy of a Blood Debt: How Clan Revenge Killings are Fracturing Somalia's Frontlines

items.title: AFRICOM Conducts Airstrike Against al-Shabaab in Somalia
items.description: According to AFRICOM, the strike took place approximately 175 kilometers west of Mogadishu as part of ongoing joint efforts to weaken al-Shabaab's operational capabilities. AFRICOM said it continues to work alongside the Somali federal government and Somali Armed Forces to degrade the militant group's ability to threaten U.S. forces and American citizens abroad. The command did not disclose specific details about the units or military assets involved, citing operational security concerns. items.title: Switzerland plans deportation of seriously injured Somali citizen
items.description: As we have learnt from two individuals affected, Swiss police authorities use an enormous amount of violence during forced deportations. From the perspective of lawyers and Swiss human rights organisations, the authorities are thereby committing massive violations of Swiss and international law. Furthermore, in at least two cases, they have put the lives of those affected at serious risk. Augenauf shares this assessment and has informed the relevant authorities (including the commander of the Zurich cantonal police and the National Commission for the Prevention of Torture, NKVF). Bot
items.titleIt: Switzerland plans deportation of seriously injured Somali citizen

items.title: Somali journalist Bashir Mohamed Abdullahi dies after being shot during Baidoa clashes
items.description: MOGADISHU, Somalia 7 September 2026 – The Somali Journalists Syndicate (SJS) expresses its deepest condolences over the death of journalist Bashir Mohamed Abdullahi, also known as Bashir Moalin, a reporter with the local Arlaadi Media Network, who succumbed to gunshot injuries sustained during armed clashes in Baidoa on Thursday, 3 September 2026. He becomes the second journalist killed in Somalia this year. Early on Monday, 7 September 2026, Bashir, 28, died from critical injuries he sustained while seeking shelter during armed clashes in Baidoa, Southwest State, his family told SJS. Accordin
items.titleIt: Somali journalist Bashir Mohamed Abdullahi dies after being shot during Baidoa clashes

items.title: Somalia: Doolow Explosions Trigger Clash of Accounts Between Jubbaland and Mogadishu
items.description: Jubbaland said General Abdirahman and members of his family were inside the residence when the explosions occurred, sustaining minor injuries before being moved to a secure location for treatment. The Somali federal government, however, has denied any involvement in the incident and offered a different account. Government officials said preliminary information gathered by security agencies indicates that the explosions were caused by materials being prepared inside the house, rather than by an external airstrike. The government's account could not immediately be independently verified. Jubbala
items.titleIt: Somalia: Doolow Explosions Trigger Clash of Accounts Between Jubbaland and Mogadishu

items.title: Somalia: How Mogadishu Removes a Regional President. It Costs Cash, or It Costs an Army
items.description: An investigation into South West State, Hirshabelle, and Galmudug found that federal governments — Farmaajo's and now Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's — have used two tools to control who governs the regions. The first is cash. The second, used once so far, is force. The First Payment In 2018, South West State's president, Sharif Hassan Sheikh Aden, stood in the way of Mogadishu's plans. He had a strong clan base and his own political network. He was not easy to remove. So Mogadishu paid him. According to sources with direct knowledge of the negotiations, Sharif Hassan received about two million US dol
items.titleIt: Somalia: How Mogadishu Removes a Regional President. It Costs Cash, or It Costs an Army

items.title: Somalia: How Sadia Bajaaj Was Convicted — Inside the Judge Swap and the Pressure Behind Her Case
items.description: According to her legal team and a review of court proceedings, a judge was swapped out mid-trial, and the Attorney General's office pushed the case at both the trial and the appeal. A Conviction That Almost Didn't Happen Sadia, a tuk-tuk driver turned social media activist, was arrested twice in 2026. The first time, on March 12, she was held four days after joining protests over rising fuel prices, then released without charge. The second arrest came April 12, when officers from Somalia's National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) detained her in Mogadishu's Hodan district. The trigger
items.titleIt: Somalia: How Sadia Bajaaj Was Convicted — Inside the Judge Swap and the Pressure Behind Her Case
